How the checking was done: Four independent checks ran in parallel on the exported results, each by a separate agent that did not share the page's code: (1) a mathematical re-solve of every design's circuit in Python/numpy, (2) a cross-case consistency check of every number and rule, with a written reason why each winner is the optimum, (3) a local-optimality test that nudged every input of every winner one and two grid steps in the real page, and (4) a visual check of all 38 pictures against the data. A fifth agent reviewed the page's code for bugs. Every bug they confirmed was fixed, the cases were re-run, and the checks were repeated on the final results.
1 · Mathematics (independent re-solve): An agent wrote its own nodal solver in Python/numpy and re-solved every design's exported circuit (the exact branches and resistances the page used), with all three phases at 360 A. Result: 0 discrepancies in all 12 designs, largest differences ≈ 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻¹¹. It reproduced every path current and path imbalance per phase, all three line-to-line resistances, every loss, each part's current and current density (J = I/A), and J max. Kirchhoff's current law holds at every node, the two coils of each series pair carry identical current, and the numbers stored by the optimiser equal the numbers measured after loading each design.
2 · Consistency and why each design is o: A second agent checked every design against every rule and against the other designs. All 12 designs are feasible (the only failing rules are the two coil-bend rules, which belong to the coil CAD). Each goal's winner has the best score for its goal among all designs that satisfy that case's rules, and every relaxation moves the right way: terminals within 60° and 90° lower the imbalance, a 15 A/mm² limit and a 6 % imbalance limit lower the copper. Masses, losses, imbalances and J are internally consistent (every part loss = I²R, every mass = length × width × thickness × density). Its written reasons are in each design's “Why this is the optimum” box.
3 · Local optimality (every input nudged: A third agent took each winner into the real page and tried 44–48 neighbours: every input ±1 and ±2 grid steps, every terminal order, every ring arrangement and every cross-section mode. In the final run 8 of 11 winners are strict local optima; the other three (balanced, least copper, J ≤ 15) can be improved by at most 0.05 % by a half-step move. The binding constraints are the same everywhere: any thicker or wider copper hits the in-plane gap and the radial limits, and the terminals are boxed by the lug pitch, the span limit and “terminal on its own ring”. Earlier rounds of this test found that the optimiser was not fully converged (up to 1.7 % left on the table) and that the 60°/90° cases could land in a worse region; both were fixed (final polish stage; earlier winners fed back as seeds).
4 · Pictures checked against the data: A fourth agent looked at all 38 pictures and compared them with the data: the cross-section style claimed (uniform / at the J limit / widened), the largest current-density label against J max and the limit, sampled area labels against each part's area (widened parts show “normal – widened” and the widened value equals t × widened width), and the terminal positions against the span. All checks pass. It found and we fixed: a wrong “widened” label on the 6 % design (nothing was widened there), area labels that hid the widening, and balancing labels overlapping terminal labels (now on the plan only; 3D shows red markers).
Bugs found during this check and fixed:
• Optimiser ignored your operating conditions (line current, temperature, joint resistances): every candidate was solved at the defaults, and loading a result overwrote your settings. Now it always uses the settings on screen.
  • Least-copper sizing leaked between designs: loading one design after another kept the previous design's sizing density (a design shown as 148 g came out as 180 g). Fixed; the “Optimised default” button also resets the section mode.
  • Custom weights: the goal table kept the scores from the run; it now recomputes every goal score when weights change.
  • Feasibility verdicts disagreed between the top strip, Checks, Results and Optimize tabs (different rule sets). All now use one verdict: every busbar rule plus the Geometry-tab limits.
  • Weld pads under-modelled when spokes are narrowed (4 mm instead of 5 mm), which overstated clearances by 0.5 mm; the weld-to-weld rule had the same 4 mm assumption. Both now use the real pad width.
  • Widened segments drawn with rounded ends in the clearance check, which reported false 2.3 mm gaps; they are now square steps, as stamped.
  • Optimiser not fully converged: winners could still be improved by 0.01–1.7 % by another section mode or a small step. A final polish stage now tries every section mode and then steps every input until nothing improves, and earlier winners are fed back in so a relaxed rule never gives a worse result.
  • Terminal gaps capped at 25°, so “terminals within” above 50° had no effect; terminal blade fixed at 10 × 3 mm, so no current-density limit below 12 A/mm² was feasible; joint resistance 0 µΩ gave NaN; the balancing switch turned itself on during re-runs; labels overlapped (balancing values, widened areas). All fixed.
Known limits of the model:
• DC/low-frequency resistive model: at speed the coil inductance dominates and evens out the path split, so the path imbalance shown is the stall (worst) case.
  • The two coil-bend rules (corner bends 26.8 %, layer-change step 35.1 % against ≤ 25 %) fail in every design: they are properties of the coil CAD, not the busbar.
  • Path balancing resistances are modelled as extra jumper wire; the routing room for that wire is not checked.
  • Widened segments are modelled as square steps; current crowding at the steps is not modelled (it slightly raises local J at the step corners).
  • The terminal blade (≥ 30 mm²) carries the full line current, so the current-density rule is set by the terminals (12.0 A/mm²) in every design.
